text: The Death of Hundun: When Our Own Wholeness Becomes the Standard for Others
The emperor of the Southern Sea was called Shu; the emperor of the Northern Sea, Hu; and the emperor of the center, Hundun.
Shu and Hu often met at Hundun’s home. Hundun treated them very well. Wanting to repay his kindness, the two discussed what to do:
People all have seven openings, for seeing, hearing, eating, and breathing. Hundun alone has none. Why not bore some for him?
Each day they bored one opening.
On the seventh day, Hundun died.
The story is short. So short that it offers no explanation, no argument, and no one to state the moral at the end.
Yet its most unsettling feature is already clear enough:
What killed Hundun was not hostility, but repayment.
Shu and Hu did not dislike Hundun.

They remembered the kindness they had received and wanted to respond. If the two characters had merely been cruelly harming a being unlike themselves, the problem would be simpler. We would only need to say they should not do it.
But they were doing it for his own good.
That makes the story much harder.

For many forces that enter another person’s life do not arrive as malice. They may begin with concern, gratitude, responsibility, even love. Someone sees another person without something they themselves possess, and naturally thinks:
Perhaps I can supply it.
The problem lies in how that judgment of “lacking” is formed.
What Shu and Hu say is: “People all have seven openings.”
At first, this describes a common appearance. But in the next step, it quietly becomes a standard:
Since everyone has them, Hundun should have them too.
Since he does not, he must be missing something.
Since he is missing something, supplying it must surely be helping him.
Between “different from us” and “incomplete,” not a single question is asked.
The story has, in fact, already given Shu and Hu an important fact about Hundun:
Hundun treated them very well.
He could welcome visitors, spend time with them, and offer kindness. However strange his way of existing might be, he was not an unresponsive lump of material waiting for others to give it shape.
But Shu and Hu did not let that fact affect their judgment.
They knew Hundun was kind to them, yet still did not consider him entitled to exist as he was. They accepted his hospitality without accepting the being who offered it.
What they saw was:
He does not have what we have.
But they did not go on to ask:
Does he suffer because of it?
Are these openings something he needs?
Might his life already work in another way?
They wanted to repay Hundun, but never let him take part in deciding what would count as repayment.
This is a very particular kind of goodwill.
It is willing to give to others, but unwilling to let them define what they need.
Helping and remaking someone sometimes involve similar actions.
Both may provide resources, change environments, develop abilities, or temporarily do for someone what they cannot do themselves.
The difference need not lie in how extensive the action is, but in where it begins.
Help usually begins with a difficulty the other person actually faces.
What do they want to accomplish?
What is getting in their way?
What kind of support would they like?
Even if they cannot express themselves clearly for now, we look as far as possible to their circumstances, reactions, and the direction they have already shown for guidance.
Remaking someone, by contrast, is more likely to begin with the helper’s own discomfort.
This person is unlike the people I know.
Their pace makes me anxious.
Their choices are hard to explain.
They are not outgoing enough, decisive enough, organized enough, ambitious enough, or they do not express affection in the way I am used to.
So we turn “I don’t know how to understand them” into “They need correcting.”
Once that happens, the other person’s difference itself becomes evidence of a problem.
The more they resist change, the more we believe they have not yet understood what is best for them.
This does not mean every change is harmful, or that staying the same is always better.
Some absences really do cause suffering.
Some abilities really do need to be developed.
When someone faces imminent danger, cannot understand the consequences, or temporarily cannot protect themselves, others may also have to intervene first and wait for full consent later.
So the death of Hundun cannot simply be rewritten as:
Do not touch anyone.
Do not help anyone.
Whatever existed originally must be preserved forever.
The story offers none of these answers.
What it really presses us to ask is something else:
**On what grounds can we be sure a change is helping someone, rather than making them more like ourselves?**
We can begin with a few very simple questions.
Does this change address a real difficulty, or merely our unease with difference?
Do we know what the other person wants to do, or have we already decided for them what is worth doing?
Can they refuse, make adjustments, or ask us to stop?
If they cannot express themselves for now, have we carefully distinguished necessary protection from taking over for the long term?
Who bears most of the consequences of the change?
And if we discover that our understanding might be wrong, are we truly prepared to stop?
These questions will not make every intervention easy.
They merely prevent good intentions from escaping scrutiny simply by calling themselves good intentions.
“Each day they bored one opening” is another weighty sentence in this story.
Hundun did not die in a single violent assault.
The change was spread across seven days, just a little each day.

Taken separately, every step looks like a small improvement. One more opening, one more ability, one more point of resemblance to everyone else. On any given day, things might not seem serious enough to require stopping.
Yet seven seemingly reasonable little steps ended up changing the entire form on which Hundun’s existence depended.
Many attempts to remake people happen this way too.
No one asks someone else to give themselves up entirely, all at once.

Just adjust the way you speak a little, then the rhythm of your life; accept a goal everyone approves of, then drop an interest that is harder to explain; learn to behave more appropriately, then gradually stop asking why you were reluctant in the first place.
A local justification can be found for every change.
Until one day a person has become easier to understand, easier to manage, and more in line with everyone’s expectations, yet finds it harder and harder to know whose life they are now living.
Gradual change is not automatically gentle change.
Some irreversible things are accomplished precisely through many steps that look small and reasonable.
Shu and Hu wanted to give Hundun more abilities.
Seeing, hearing, eating, and breathing are all important functions of life. So the story also touches on another very modern question:
Do more abilities always mean a better existence?
It is easy to mistake addition for improvement.
Knowing more, reacting faster, expressing ourselves more clearly, having more choices, adapting to more environments. Many additions do, of course, genuinely enlarge our lives.
But abilities are not components that can be fitted into a person without limit.

A new ability changes an existing way of life; a new standard of evaluation changes where attention goes; a more efficient way of expressing something may leave an experience once difficult to articulate with only the part most conveniently understood.
The real question is not only “Can they do one more thing?” It also includes:
What has a person been changed into in order to acquire this ability?
Have they gained more possibilities of their own, or merely become better suited to purposes others have already prepared for them?
Shu and Hu did not see this distinction.
For them, adding was itself improving, and being like everyone else was itself being whole.
With his death, Hundun demonstrated:
The wholeness one form of life needs cannot necessarily be copied directly from the shape of another.
Of course, we do not know how Hundun would have answered.
The story does not let him speak, nor does it tell us whether he resisted, whether he felt pain, or whether he had already changed after the first day.
We cannot fill that silence however we please.
We cannot say on his behalf that he loved the way he was; nor can we say that he actually wanted to change and only the method of remaking him went wrong.
But the story leaves us at least one fact:
Before Shu and Hu began to “perfect” him, Hundun was already able to be kind to others in his own way.
That makes him more than a blank waiting to be defined.
It also makes Shu and Hu’s judgment all the more jarring.
They accepted the good Hundun gave them, but did not treat his way of existing as a fact worth taking seriously.
They wanted to repay someone without first acknowledging:
The other person may know better than we do, in our efforts to repay them, what kind of life remains a life for them.
Perhaps goodwill’s most common mistake is not doing too little.
It is believing too quickly that it already knows what the other person lacks.

We take the familiar for the normal, the common for the complete, and the lives we can understand for the lives worth living. Then, in the name of help, education, care, or gratitude, we begin boring entrances to something “better” for other people.
Some entrances really do bring light and air.
Others merely make it easier for us to look in from outside.
Hundun’s story does not ask us to stop helping.
It leaves us only a stern reminder:
Before setting out to perfect another person, first ask whether what we see is their incompleteness, or simply the fact that they have not grown into our shape.
Shu and Hu wanted to fill Hundun out, to make him more complete.
But what they really added was only themselves.
And what they took away was the possibility of Hundun continuing to exist in Hundun’s own way.

*Textual basis: the fable of “the death of Hundun” at the end of “Responding to Emperors and Kings” in the Zhuangzi. This essay addresses only the questions of goodwill, difference, and remaking others presented by this fable itself. It is not offered as a complete interpretation of the Zhuangzi as a whole or of Zhuangzi’s philosophy.*
